## What models to use when

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
`lm()`: Linear models

- OLS regression
- *t*-tests
- ANOVA
- Multiple regression
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
`lme()`, `lmer()`, `glmmTMB()`

- Multilevel linear models
- Others ([CRAN Mixed Models Task View](https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/MixedModels.html))

:::

::::


## What models to use when

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Generalized linear models

- `glm()`
    - Logistic (binomial)
    - Poisson (counts)
    - Other distributions
- Zero-inflated binomial and counts
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Generalized linear *mixed* models

- `glmer()`
- `glmmTMB()`
- Others ([CRAN Mixed Models Task View](https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/MixedModels.html))

:::

::::


## Best practices {.smaller}

> My question is about communicating the importance of visualizing and understanding data prior to analysis, as well as utilizing different and comparing models.

> I hear a lot of, "Just analyze the data after you've collected it." It is good to start looking at data once collected, but now that I have better knowledge and all these tools, do you have a recommendation about how to approach PIs or lab mates about the steps that come before analysis? Doing it the right way can take longer, but it amounts to more robust science.
